38 /**
39 * @brief Fortran/Column-major stride order.
40 * @details The first dimension varies the fastest, the last dimension the slowest.
41 * @tparam Rank Number of dimensions.
42 */
43 template <int Rank>
44 constexpr uint64_t Fortran_stride_order = nda::encode(nda::permutations::reverse_identity<Rank>());
45
46 /**
47 * @brief C/Row-major stride order.
48 * @details The last dimension varies the fastest, the first dimension the slowest.
49 * @tparam Rank Number of dimensions.
50 */
51 template <int Rank>
52 constexpr uint64_t C_stride_order = nda::encode(nda::permutations::identity<Rank>());
53
54 /**
55 * @brief Layout that specifies how to map multi-dimensional indices to a linear/flat index.
56 *
57 * @details It stores the shape of the array, i.e. the length of each dimension, and the strides of each dimension.
58 * The stride of dimension `i` is the number of elements to skip in memory when the index of dimension `i` is
59 * incremented by one. For example:
60 * - To iterate over every element of a 5x5x5 array in C-order use the strides `(25, 5, 1)`.
61 * - To iterate over every 2nd element of a 1D array use the stride `(2)`.
62 * - To iterate over every 2nd column of a 10x10 array in Fortran-order use the strides `(1, 20)`.
63 * - To iterate over every 2nd row of a 10x10 array in Fortran-order use the strides `(2, 10)`.
64 *
65 * The template parameters `StaticExtents` and `StrideOrder` are encoded as `uint64_t`. They can be decoded to a

289 std::array<long, Rank> extents;

582 * @brief Create a new map by permuting the indices/dimensions of the current map with a given permutation.
583 *
584 * @details Let \f$ A \f$ be the current and \f$ A' \f$ the new, permuted index map. \f$ P \f$ is the given
585 * permutation. We define the permuted nda::idx_map \f$ A' \f$ to be the one with the following properties:
586 * - \f$ A'(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1}) = A(i_{P[0]},\ldots,i_{P[n-1]}) \f$
587 * - \f$ A'.\text{lengths}()[k] = A.\text{lengths}()[P^{-1}[k]] \f$
588 * - \f$ A'.\text{strides}()[k] = A.\text{strides}()[P^{-1}[k]] \f$
589 * - The stride order of \f$ A' \f$ is the composition of \f$ P \f$ and the stride order of \f$ A \f$ (note that
590 * the stride order itself is a permutation).

600 //
601 // Note that this convention is the correct one to have a (left) action of the symmetric group on
602 // an array and it may not be completely obvious.
603 // Proof
604 // let's operate with P then Q, and denote A'' = Q A'. We want to show that A'' = (QP) A
605 // A'(i_k) = A(i_{P[k]})
606 // A''(j_k) = A'(j_{Q[k]})
607 // then i_k = j_{Q[k]} and A''(j_k) = A(i_{P[k]}) = A(j_{Q[P[k]]}) = A(j_{(QP)[k]}), q.e.d

613 //
614 // where S[k] denotes the strides.
615 //
616 // 1- S' : strides of A'
617 // A'(i_k) = sum_k i_{P[k]} * S[k] = sum_k i_k * S[P^{-1}[k]]
618 // so
619 // S'[k] = S[P^{-1}[k]] (2)
620 // i.e. apply (inverse(P), S) or apply_inverse directly.
621 //
622 // 2- L' : lengths of A'
623 // if L[k] is the k-th length, then because of the definition of A', i.e. A'(i_k) = A(i_{P[k]})
624 // i_q in the lhs A is at position q' such that P[q'] = q (A'(i0 i1 i2...) = A( i_P0 i_P1 i_P2....)
625 // hence L'[q] = L[q'] = L[P^{-1}[q]]
626 // same for static length
627 //
628 // 3- stride_order: denoted in this paragraph as Q (and Q' for A').
629 // by definition Q is a permutation such that Q[0] is the slowest index, Q[Rank -1] the fastest
630 // hence S[Q[k]] is a strictly decreasing sequence (as checked by strides_compatible_to_stride_order)
631 // we want therefore Q' the permutation that will sort the S', i.e.

633 // using (2), we have S[P^{-1}[Q'[k]]] = S[Q[k]]
634 // so the permutation Q' is such that P^{-1}Q' = Q or Q' = PQ (as permutation product/composition).
635 // NB : Q and P are permutations, so the operation must be a composition, not an apply (apply applies
636 // P to any set, like L, S, not only a permutation) even though they are all `std::array` in the code ...
